One ruler of this polity diluted his power by placing his brother Pacorus in control of a region of Atropatene and attempted to the found the anti-Greek town of Vologesias. An earlier king of this empire may have partially ruled with his son, also named Pacorus, and killed his father before the latter could respond to the occupation of Orsoene and Gordyene. That king, Orodes II, also put to death, the victorious general in a battle over Gaius Cassius Longinus and others. Its first capital was likely centered at Dara, and this polity's rule was ended by Ardashir I. Before that, one king of this polity defeated Artavases of Armenia but was himself defeated by the Scythians; that man was Mithridates the Great. Defeating Marcus Licinius Crassus at the battle of Carrhae, name this Mesopotamian empire, a rival of Rome.

Battles in this conflict included one named for Kilometer 7 and another where the Vickers Rifles taken from the slain enemy were placed back on their corpses, the Second Battle of Nanawa. The inept handling of this war led Germán Busch to launch a coup against the loser's president. The victors in this conflict relied on the foreign expertise of Generals Belaieff and Porfeneko, while the losers were helped by the German Hans Kundt. Because they failed to obtain a victor's peace, the victorious side saw President Eusebio Ayala and Jose Felix Estgarribia deposed after it ended. The victors also made heavy use of Guarani troops native to the contested territory. Name this South American conflict over a namesake region thought to be rich in oil.

[5,5] For 5 points per answer, name the two nations who bailed out their citizens who had had deposits in Icelandic banks, and were understandably nonplussed when Icelandic voters recently voted not to pay them back.

The Langemark war cemetery memorializes those who died during battles named for this place. An incident in which several German units were killed by a small force of experienced Boer War veterans occurred at a battle named for this polity and is called "The Massacre of the Innocents of" this place. A later battle at this place was led primarily to cripple German submarine warfare by capturing German port cities but proved inconclusive, in part because the area surrounding this city was located on reclaimed marshland which turned to thick mud after being repeatedly shelled, and it also marked the first use of poison gas on the Western Front. Name this Belgian city, site of multiple World War I battles.

The term of the first president of this country, Charles Debbas, was extended by one year after a proposal to break an electoral deadlock involving Emile Iddi. Iddi would later become the last president of this country under French control, which ended after the Battle of Damour in this country; a subsequent battle led to the Armistice of Acre. That French control had been guaranteed by the terms of the Sykes-Picot Treaty, and it was given its mandate over this country at the San Remo conference. Its National Pact established a division of power along its confessional cleavages, with the office of Prime Minister being reserved for Sunnis and the presidency being given to the Maronite majority. Name this country, whose fifteen-year civil war saw invasions by both Israel and Syria, whose capital is Beirut.

This was predated by the First System run by the Iberian nations and was a closed system closely controlled by the state. Sometimes called the Maafa, V.S. Naipul wrote of its aftereffects in a book named for it. The last known ship to participate in it was the Clotilde, which sailed to Mobile, Alabama. Another ship that sailed it was depicted by J. M. W. Turner in a painting, and Robert Hayden wrote a poem with its name. The actions of the captain of the Zong became notorious in it, and proved a catalyst for people including William Wilberforce to help outlaw it in Great Britain. Another participating ship, whose "cargo" was freed by an 1831 Supreme Court case, was La Amistad. Name this leg of the Atlantic triangular trade, which used manufactured goods from Europe to buy slaves and sold them for raw materials in the Americas.

This man was severely wounded as a major at the Battle of the Monongahela, and he served as an aide to Robert Monckton during his capture of Martinique, also during the Seven Years War. This man was supposedly the choice of the "Conway Cabal" to lead the armies of the nation he served, although he did get a chance to lead all of the southern armies, a role in which he was less successful as he had been previously, commanding a decisive defeat at the Battle of Camden. Earlier, he had taken over from Phillip Schuyler just in time to take credit for victories won mostly by the actions of John Stark and Benedict Arnold, at Bennington and Freeman's Farm. Who was this American general who took credit for the victory at the Battle of Saratoga?

He was born in a prison cell on a day known as Janmashtami, shortly followed by his supernatural escape to the care of his foster parents in Vrindavana. Upon rescuing the 16,000 maidens held by the demon Narakasura, he married all of them in order to preserve their social status. Often depicted as a child eating butter or playing the flute, he held a hill up above the residents of his town to shelter them from a storm. Duryodhana chose this deity's army for the Kauravas after he refused to raise a weapon in the Kurukshetra. The Pandavas, however, chose him as he served as Arjuna's charioteer, to whom he delivered the Bhagavad Gita. Name this incarnation of Vishnu, generally shown alongside his consort, Radha.

This case's decision is almost always cited along with the Panama Refining case, specifically by Byron White in INS v. Chadha where he noted "restrictions on the scope of the power that could be delegated… have all but disappeared." Though its underlying principle was seemingly supported by the previous year's Home Building and Loan v. Blaisdell, Justice Cardozo agreed with Hughes' statement in this decision that "extraordinary conditions" do not create or enlarge constitutional power. Derided by the sitting president as a "horse and buggy" interpretation of the Constitution, and affecting the drafting of the National Labor Relations Act, name this 1935 case, a dagger in FDR's NIRA, that revolved wage, hour and quality conditions at some Brooklyn slaughterhouses.
Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States

One of his former lieutenants, who had switched sides before rejoining his side, won the Battle of Vertieres. That lieutenant had defected to the side led by Charles Leclerc, who would force this man's surrender, and trick him into imprisonment, where he died of pneumonia. Before Leclerc was sent, however, this man had allied with Sonthonax, then forced him out, and negotiated with the British and Americans to leave him alone in exchange for sugar and promises not to invade Jamaica or the American South. Assisted by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who was this man who led the first successful slave revolt in the New World, liberating what would become Haiti?

This organization organized a boycott involving white stickers to demonstrate their opposition to immigration from a certain country. This organization was founded after a dispute when part of another similar organization broke a cigar makers' strike in New York by undercutting the strikers' wage demands; a member of the striking union would become this group's first president. One initiative pursued under his leadership was the placing of white stickers of cigars made by white workers in opposition to Chinese immigration. A breakaway faction of this group focused on industry, founded by John L. Lewis, as opposed to the initial focus on craft, would eventually rejoin in 1955. Identify this labor union, which merged with the Congress of Industrial Organizations and was founded by, among others, Samuel Gompers.

This group emerged during disputes with the self-styled "True Protestants", in turn referring to themselves as the Abhorrers. Initial success in that conflict was exemplified by the crushing of the Monmouth Rebellion. The prosecution of preacher Henry Sacheverell and the namesake disturbances led to another of this group's successes, the creation of the Riot Act, thirty years after their defeat of the Exclusion Act. Cromwell's conquests during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms led to the phenomenon that named this party, by causing an increase in landless, armed Irish-Catholics. It declined from its heyday, when led by such figures as William Pitt the Younger, to a small surviving faction headed by Benjamin Disraeli that became its spiritual successor, the modern Conservative Party. Rising to prominence due to their defense of royal power during the English Restoration, this is, what British political party, which was opposed by the Whigs?

The Greeks Megasthenes and Deimachus were sent as ambassadors to the first and second rulers of this polity. Demetrius I of Bactria began his devastating invasion of this empire after a coup overthrew their last ruler; his new empire would share the region with the Sunga Empire founded by the leader of that coup. The first ruler of this empire was advised by the author of a treatise on statecraft called the Arthashastra, Chanakya. That ruler consolidated his power by defeating Magadha, and he left a vast empire to his son Bindusara. This empire's third ruler was so sickened by his expansive military conquests that he built thousands of stupas and famously converted to Buddhism. Name this Indian empire founded by Chandragupta and later ruled by Asoka.

The OKH rejected a plan to lure the Soviets into the Donets River basin, there to be trapped against the Sea of Azov, instead selecting the brainchild of Chief of Staff Zeitzler over Field Marshal von Manstein. This maneuver, which reached its climax at the Battle of Prokhorovka, was in the Kesselschlacht concept, with the two prongs coming from Orel and Karkhov. Operation Citadel was delayed at Hitler's order multiple times before execution, and Stavka and Georgy Zhukov had to convince Stalin to take advantage of the information garnered by the Lucy spy ring, and wait until the Germans launched their predictable assault against one of the most heavily entrenched salient on earth. Marking the debut of a vehicle to counter the Soviet T-34, name this battle in which the Panther tank first appeared, the costliest single day of aerial warfare and the largest tank battle in history.

The CIA initiated Project RAINBOW in an attempt to keep this from being detected. Although this project ultimately failed, it did lead to the development of the A-12. Plans to retire this vehicle have been postponed to at least 2012 or 2014 to allow for additional time to ready its replacement, the RQ-4. Originally powered by Pratt & Whitney J57 engines, this vehicle is exceedingly difficult to operate, since it was designed for rapid flight at high altitudes with its long, thin wings. On October 14, 1962, one of these aircraft was responsible for capturing images of the Soviet military installing nuclear missiles in Cuba, sparking to the Cuban Missile Crisis. Name this reconnaissance aircraft, which became well known after a CIA pilot was shot down in one over Soviet territory on May 1st, 1960, resulting in the capture of Francis Gary Powers.

John Penruddock led an uprising during this period that led to the nation's division into military districts, which were controlled by Army Major Generals. During this time, a war was ended that led to the signing of the Treaty of Westminster, as Admiral Robert Blake's forces won the Battle of Scheveningen to end the First Anglo-Dutch War. One of the generals in that war, George Monck, would prove instrumental in ending this period, as he eventually used his forces to allow the seating of a new Parliament and accepting the issuance of the Declaration of Breda, in which the conditions for retaking the throne were laid out by Charles Stuart. Name this period of English history, during which it was under the rule of the Lord Protectors Richard, and his father Oliver, Cromwell.

This battle took place on Kalkriese Hill during torrential rains, which prevented one from using their sinew-string bows and waterlogged shields. They fell into a trap at the foot of the hill, where the road was narrow, sandwiched between the Great Bog on one side and the hill on the other, and it was also blocked by a trench, and ran near a wall from behind which the enemies attacked. They had been led to that hill by false rumors of rebellion started by the leader of the enemy side, and were ambushed by members of the Cherusci, Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri, Chauci, and Sicambri tribes, who united under Arminius. Name this 9 A.D. Battle in which an alliance of Germanic tribes under Arminius defeated Romans under Publius Quinctilius Varus, also known as the Varian disaster.

The Holmec Incident, in which JNA troops were supposedly killed while attempting to surrender, occurred during this country's war of independence of a namesake length. At the end of the Ten-Day War, this country signed the Brioni Agreement. The Julian Alps, Kamnik-Savinja Alps, and the Karavanke chain can be found in this country, which also has a region that gives its name to a type of topography, the Kras Plateau. This country contains part of the Drava River, a tributary of the Danube, on which the largest city in the country's region of Lower Styria lies. That city is also home to this country's second largest airport, Maribor Airport. It recently joined the European Union, becoming, in 2008, the first ex-Communist country to hold the Presidency of the Council of that body. This is, what Slavic nation that was formerly a part of Yugoslavia, and whose capital is at Ljubljana?

During his reign, his polity's forces won the Battle of Watling Street, crushing a revolt that had already sacked present-day Colchester and London. Another revolt against him was nearly busted by the efforts of one woman to recruit sailors to the cause; she strangled herself rather than reveal her co-conspirators under torture. He sent Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo to negotiate peace with the Parthian Empire, although he would eventually order Corbulo and two of his own advisors to commit suicide, Petronius and Seneca. This man also appointed a future emperor to put down a revolt in Judea; he would use the same forces to eventually accede to the throne after a year of chaos. Succeeded by Galba after his suicide triggered the Year of Four Emperors, this is, what nephew of Claudius, a Roman Emperor who probably didn't fiddle while Rome burned?

By the end of this battle, the height of one hill had been lowered by 4 meters, rendering its name inaccurate. Assaults against Côte 304 and the hills of Le Mort Homme were successful, and allowed the attackers to shift their focus to the right bank of the river and further gains. Those gains were eventually surrendered in November, preceding the defenders' recapture of Fort Douaumont, near which a prior defense by the 33rd Infantry Regiment had allowed the safe passage of massive quantities of materiel by trucks on the "Voie Sacree", or "Sacred Road." During that action company commander Charles De Gaulle was captured. In choosing the battle site, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed the French would attempt an absolute defense of the historically significant surrounding forts, though he expected the toll of casualties to weigh in the Germans' favor. Name, this battle fought in 1916 during World War I in which the Germans attempted to "bleed the French white."

The burning of a ship that had been supplying rebels by Canadian loyalists caused this man to protest to Great Britain, to no avail. His second running mate, the grandson of a previous president, was Charles Francis Adams, Sr. He first proposed the establishment of an independent treasury in response to a crisis brought on in part by the demise of the Second Bank of the United States, although his proposals were defeated in Congress. In addition to sending Cherokees from Georgia to present-day Oklahoma on the Trail of Tears, this man had to deal with Caroline affair and the Panic of 1837. A candidate for President in 1848 under the Free Soil banner, who was this eighth President of the United States?

He published a number of scientific papers on hydroids, and discovered several new species of Hydrozoa. He was named an honorary field marshal of the British army, and named a Knight of the Order of Garter, although these honors were revoked, then later restored. He became regent after his father Taisho became ill, and his death marked the start of the Heisei period. On becoming Emperor, he decided to call his regnal period the Showa era, meaning "peace and enlightenment," but this name was turned into a bad joke by events like the Mukden incident and the Second Sino-Japanese War, as well as the actions of his prime minister Hideki Tojo. This is, what Emperor of Japan during World War II?

This man's government withdrew recognition from a government that would be defeated at the Second Battle of Rivas by Costa Ricans and mercenaries supported by Cornelius Vanderbilt. Deliberations held in Belgium would prove embarrassing to him, and this man's Secretary of War would go on to serve in a higher office for another country. One piece of legislation that he signed was designed to open up land for a continental railroad, but the aftermath of the signing saw Preston Brooks' caning of Charles Sumner as well as the Pottawatomie Massacre. Who is this man, who appointed Jefferson Davis to his cabinet, and, presided over the drafting of a document stating plans to annex Cuba, the Ostend Manifesto, signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act and lost the 1856 Democratic nomination to James Buchanan?

The assassination of Orlando Letelier on foreign soil on the orders of this man proved embarrassing to a group that had helped him to power, after Henry Kissinger had assailed his country's voters as "irresponsible" for potentially allowing Communism. Hernan Buchi was appointed by him to try to reverse the effects of his earlier economic policies; the so-called "miracle" of the country that he led, came with a reversal of the socialist policies of his predecessor, brought on by economists educated at a namesake American university. The work of the "Chicago Boys" ended abruptly with a debt crisis in 1982, and according to the Valech Report, about 28,000 people were tortured by the regime of this man. Who was this man who, in a CIA-sponsored coup in 1973, overthrew Salvador Allende as President of Chile?

Because one side was celebrating its commander's twenty-fifth birthday the night before this battle, the other side attempted a night attack but was forced to abandon its plans and retreat because of the imminent dawn. As a result of this, the losing side was exhausted, and George Murray's shift of the right wing of that side proved unheeded by the Duke of Perth and others, leaving the lines severely stretched. The commander of the government forces had arrived a few months before this battle after the previous blunders of Cope and Hawley that failed to quell the conflict. A combination of the government forces' superior artillery and the marshy and uneven terrain made the famed Highland charge much less effective. Name this battle, where the Duke of Cumberland faced Charles Edward Stuart, the last battle of the Jacobite Rising of 1745 and the last battle fought on British soil.

The influence of the Nok culture is thought to have addressed one of the most salient features of this event to the people of the Benue Valley. The southernmost participants of this event were affected by areal diffusion of click consonants from the Khoisan, and this event is posited to have followed two routes, the western of which saw the settlement of the rain forests and the eastern of which saw travel through the savannahs into the Great Lakes area and Great Rift Valley and points south. Thought to have originated in Cameroon and tied to the spread of iron-smelting and agricultural development, this is, what mass movement of speakers of Niger-Congo languages across most of sub-Saharan Africa?

Kings Mindaugas II and Charles I came to the thrones of their countries as a result of this agreement. One of the side-effects of this was repulsed by the "Miracle of the Vistula", and finally resolved by the Treaty of Riga, while an indirect result of this was the defeat of the Red Guards at Tampere, as one group was unable to provide direct support to one side of the Finnish Civil War, although they were able to fight the Polish-Soviet War. This agreement, nullified by the Treaty of Rapallo, was negotiated primarily by Richard von Kuhlmann on one side, and Leon Trotsky on the other. Resulting in a loss of one-quarter of Russia's population, name this treaty signed in March 1918 that effectively withdrew Russia from World War I.

The flagship of the task force led by Aubrey Fitch was sunk after this battle because gasoline vapors released by a torpedo strike ignited into a fire that prevented salvage. The flagship of Frank Fletcher, which had just come from contesting the invasion of Tulagi, also suffered major damage. Weather conditions had alternately provided both sides with cover from aerial attack, though one beneficiary of the cover still lost enough planes that it had to withdraw from the theater, along with another heavily damaged carrier. Though damage to Fletcher's ship was so severe that the Admiral Shigeyoshi Inoue was informed it had been sunk, repairs were made that allowed the aircraft of the Yorktown to play a crucial role a month later. The Lexington was lost, while the effective disablement of the Zuikaku and Shokaku kept them out of the Battle of Midway. What was this naval battle, the first in which enemy ships never saw each other, that prevented the invasion of Port Moresby and Australia by the Japanese in May 1942?

Calder v. Bull extended the results of this case to the states, and it was first applied in Little v. Barreme, also known as the "Flying Fish" case. Cases arising from the decision of this case include one about the President's power to seize control of steel mills during a war, Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, and one about the extent of executive privilege, United States v. Nixon. The author of the majority opinion wrote "an act of the legislature repugnant to the Constitution is void," as the Court ruled in favor of the plantiff's right to his commission as an appeals judge, but against the right of the Court to force its delivery by the Secretary of State. Identify this Supreme Court case that saw the first use of the doctrine of judicial review.

Only one ruler of this group was later recognized as a caliph and not merely a secular king; that ruler is Abd al-Aziz. His father dealt with the rebellions by al-Mukhtar in Kufa and the combined forces of the Kharijites, Shi'ah, and Abd Allah ibn az-Zubayr in Iraq. This group was split between the Sufyanids, whose first leader attempted the first siege of Constantinople, and the Marwanids, whose last ruler, Marwan II, died at the Battle of the Great Zab River. They "won" the first Muslim civil war, beating out Muhammad's son-in-law, Ali, and Mu'awiyah, the son of Abu Sufyan, was the first ruler of this polity. Ruling out of Damascus, what is this second Islamic caliphate?

One non-territorial concession of this agreement was the transfer of the Asiento to the power that also received undivided control over St. Kitts. Another power had its control over the land between the Amazon and Oyapock rivers recognized by the power that also returned to it Colonia del Sacramento, a territory in Uruguay. France agreed to destroy its fortifications at Dunkirk while Victor Amadeus II became king of Sicily and Nice. The host country was told by the French delegate that that negotiations would be held "about you, in your country, without you," and indeed the host nation received little more than the Barrier Treaties. Britain suzerainty over the Iroquois was recognized, and gained territories that increased the holdings of the Hudson Bay Company from France, who agreed to recognize the legitimacy of Queen Anne. Identify this series of treaties that concluded the War of the Spanish Succession.

The first battle in this conflict occurred just outside Calama, and witnessed the demise of Eduardo Abaroa, who made his reputation in that engagement, the Battle of Topáte. This conflict began in part due to a tax placed on a nitrate and railway company, and escalated after the outing of an alliance between nations led Mariano Prado and Hilarión Daza. Manuel González' victory at Tacna effectively removed Bolivia from this conflict less than a year after forces led by Juan Jose Latorre killed Peruvian naval hero Miguel Grau and captured his ship, the Huáscar, at the Battle of Angamos. Officially ended by the Treaty of Ancón, name this conflict, nicknamed the Saltpeter War, which saw Peru ally with Bolivia in a border dispute with Chile over mineral-rich territory.

The fantastically named Foster McGowan Voorhees held this post at the turn of the 20th century, and earlier the loser in the 1864 presidential election, George McClellan, served a single term as it. One of its more accomplished occupants served two terms in the 1980s before chairing the 9/11 Commission. In addition to Thomas Kean, one former holder of this position was famously photographed frisking Sherron Rolax, a photo which drew criticism from civil rights groups. After that controversy, she moved from this post to the EPA, but unlike Christine Todd Whitman, another former holder of this position saw his career go down in flames after an affair with Golan Cipel, who was notably a man. The former post of Jim McGreevey, name this occupation, which recently changed hands when Chris Christie replaced Jon Corzine following a 2009 election.

A bitter personal attack by Sir Earle Page on the floor of the House created a rift between this man and Page, as he accused this man of cowardice for not serving in World War I. In perhaps his most famous speech, he referred to the "middle class who, properly regarded, represent the backbone of this country," a speech titled "The Forgotten People." A virulent anti-Communist, he harnessed a Communist-backed coal strike to a decisive defeat of Labor Prime Minister Ben Chifley, and then rode the post-war boom to an unprecedented 15 years as prime minister. The founder of the Australian Liberal Party, name this longest-serving Australian prime minister.

He saw the passage of bills that would prohibit clergymen from coming within five miles of parishes that they had been banished from as well as a bill that required municipal officeholders to swear allegiance. In addition to the Five Mile Act and the Corporation Act, he also saw the foundation of an alliance with Portugal, since the Portuguese were abandoned by the French after the Treaty of the Pyrenees. He also awarded eight Lord Proprietors land that would become Carolina. Titus Oates' false confession greatly increased anti-Catholic sentiment with what would be called the "Popish Plot." This anti-Catholic sentiment would be further tested when Parliament attempted to prevent his brother from succeeding to the throne with the Exclusion Bill. Name this English monarch who rose to power because of the Restoration.

Before this battle, one side drew up their lines near Tockwith believing that the attackers were going to cross the river Nidd, while in fact they feinted and crossed the Ouse river and camped in the Galtres forest. The next morning the attacking army converged on Nether Poppleton while Lord Goring entered York to personally relieve the city from the Marquess of Newcastle. Lord Goring almost won this battle, until Lord Fairfax rode through enemy lines to muster a cavalry charge from his commander that cut down thousands of "Whitecoats." Prince Rupert was defeated by the Parliamentarian cavalry in, what 1644 victory for Oliver Cromwell that secured Northern England and was the largest battle of the English Civil War?

This work criticized an institution as being "ranked in the scriptures as one of the sins about the Jews." Furthermore, it criticizes the supporters of constitutional monarchy, arguing that in a certain country "the crown hath engrossed the commons." However, it also simplified the views of John Locke by stating "Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness," while also referring to the "natural principles" the author believed needed defending. Selling over 100,000 copies in its first year it declared that a certain conflict was "in great measure the cause of mankind" and advocated a declaration of independence. Name this 1776 radical pamphlet calling for Americans to declare independence by Thomas Paine.

Joao II sent an envoy to this ruler, possibly encouraged by a report of a prior letter received by Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Comnenus. Otto of Freising was eager to ask him to reattempt an endeavor frustrated by the flooding of the Tigris, namely an excursion from his capital at Ecbatana in Persia to capture Jerusalem. This "king of the Three Indies" had an army of 140,000 cavalry and 100,000 infantry, and his grandson David's conquests in Persia and Iraq encouraged the Bishop of Acre until it was discovered that this was actually the work of Genghis Khan. The Ethiopians were just as confused when the Christian states of Europe insisted that this man was their Emperor. Name this mythical Nestorian Christian priest-king who supposedly ruled an isolated and wealthy kingdom east of the Muslim lands.

Negotiations for this treaty began in the aftermath of the war caused by the Social Democrat government's refusal to accept the terms of the Vix Note. Instead of agreeing, that government ceded power to a party organized in a Moscow hotel just after the after the Aster Revolution, which was in turn was overthrown after losing the war with its eastern neighbor. The victors helped establish an Anti-Communist government which was still barely privy to the discussions that would remove five of its ten largest cities. Territorial losses from this treaty were somewhat recovered via two Vienna awards in 1939 and 1940 and the Munich Conference. Territories such as Vojvodina, Carpathian Ruthenia, and Transylvania were separated from the losing country, even though those territories had substantial Magyar populations. Name this treaty signed in 1920 between the Allies and Hungary, which stripped it of almost three-quarters of its territory.

During this dynasty, Quánzh?u replaced Gu?ngzh?u as the major seaport. The second emperor of this dynasty conquered Wú Yuè before capturing Tài yuán to end the Northern Hàn dynasty.The Chinese first used paper money and Zh? X? Founded Neo-Confucianism during this dynasty, which also featured the first extensive use of the Imperial civil service to pick qualified bureaucrats and the reform minded chancellor Wáng ?nshí. Originally troubled by the Khitans under the Liáo, the Jurchens soon proved to be a much greater threat. The Jurchen J?n dynasty's sack of Biàn j?ng or K?if?ng forced the evacuation of the capital to Hángzh?u, which chronologically divides this dynasty into a Northern and a Southern part. Name this dynasty founded by Tàiz? That followed the Táng Dynasty and was destroyed by the Mongols.

The night before this event, a proposed leaflet commanding one group to "appear in full force" and with "arms" was rejected. During that same night, a plan to retaliate with simultaneous bombing was discussed. That night was called the "Monday Night Conspiracy." Most of the casualties on one side were due to friendly-fire in the dark and those people died after Samuel Fielden finished a speech at 10:30 PM. Louis Lingg was one person convicted for causing this event and he survived six hours after a smuggled cigar-shaped dynamite cap blew his face off. Judge Joseph Gary sentenced Albert Parson, George Engel, and August Spies to hangings for their parts in this event, which also saw the death of Mathias Degan. Pardons for three others were signed by Illinois Governor John Altgeld for, what event where a bomb was hurled at policemen in an important commercial square in Chicago?

Early in this man's political career, due to the efforts of the Earl of Oxford and Lord Bolingbroke, he was accused of corruption and sentenced to the Tower of London for six months. Very late in his career, he passed an act that forced all plays to be preapproved by the Lord Chamberlain; the Licensing Act was partly due to his portrayal as the despicable Mr. Peachum. One important supporter of this man had prevented her husband from dismissing this man; she was Queen Caroline. His influence decreased after starting a war due to a man's lost ear during a Spanish ship inspection. Earlier, this man restored confidence in the government finances after a certain company's stocks had crashed after rising from 128? To over 1000? In 8 months. Name this man who started the War of Jenkin's Ear and dealt with the South Sea Bubble, the first British Prime Minister.

During one failed expedition, this man, on the advice of a woman named Timo, attempted to sneak into a city via a sanctuary to the goddess Kore and her mother. That incident happened during the siege of Paros. Earlier in his life, he conquered Lemnos after local Thracian tribes had made this man the tyrant of Chersonese. This man was tried for the Paros expedition and fined 50 talents, but died before he was able to pay that fine. That fine was paid by his son who defeated over 200 Phoenician ships at Eurymedon and was named Cimon. Although originally imprisoned for being a tyrant, this man's involvement in the Ionian Revolt against the Persians allowed him to be elected strategoi in 490BC. He also succeeded in convincing five other strategoi and Callimachus to attack the Persians directly instead of waiting for the Spartans. Name this general who commanded the Greek forces at Marathon.

This man's arrest corresponded with the appointment of Naevius Sutorius Macro, and this man was betrayed by his subordinate Satrius Secundus near the end of his life. This man's uncle Junius Blaesus put down the rebellion of Tacfarinas. He managed to seduce Livilla into slowly poisoning one of his rivals, and he put down a revolt in Pannonia with the help of future rival Drusus the Younger. Originally of the equestrian class and executed by being thrown down the Gemonian stairs and torn apart, this man assumed de facto power following his master's retirement to Capri. Name this prefect of the Praetorian guard who assumed power during the reign of Tiberius.

The case Rice v. Norman Williams Co regarded the ability of this act to invalidate a California law that prohibited liquor import, and it immediately followed the passage of the Valentine Act in its proposer's home state. Violations of this law can be sorted into "per se" and "rule of reason" violations. It was upheld by a case that held that a contract violates this law if it results in undue restraint, known as Standard Oil Company vs. United States. One of its first applications was settling the Pullman Strike, and it was also used to break up the Northern Securities Company and the American Tobacco Company. This event was the subject of Security Council Resolution 120, and one of the complaints during this event was the banning of the MEFESZ organization. This man's opponents formed the Lichfield House Compact in order to consolidate their power, and his government ordered that factories be cleaned every fourteenth month and that women and children couldn't work more than 12 hours a day in the Factory Act. The gift of an elephant prompted Leo X to issue Praecelsae devotionis, which partially abrogated it in favor of an earlier papal declaration, Nicholas V's Romanus pontifex. A besa, suspending all blood feuds in this nation, had to be called before the Congress of Lushnje could be held after World War I, declaring an end to the Durres Government. In 1997, anarchy spurred an Italian-led peacekeeping mission in, what formerly autarkic Balkan nation which was led until 1985 by Enver Hoxha?

The McKnight-James party made the first attempt along its dangerous "Middle Crossing" of in 1821, though the shorter "Jornada" crossing is more dangerous branch. Following the incursion of Charles Warfield and Jacob Snively's "Battalion of Invincibles" and the murder of Don Antonio Jose Chavez, Santa Ana temporarily closed it. This man largely retired from active duty after he developed heat stroke at Monmouth and he successfully engineered a retreat under Israel Putnam from Manhattan. As a youth he was sent to Rome where he was made either consul or king by Pope Leo IV and he was later responsible for reorganizing the fyrd. Identify this first King of the Anglo-Saxons, the only English king to be known as "the Great".

This clan's interpretation of biblical law led them to reject immortality of the soul and resurrection, and their rejection of the application of purity laws to anyone outside the Temple and its priests led their antagonists to consider their women menstrually impure. Their main dispute with those rivals was this clan's rejection of oral law and all practices not named in the Pentateuch. With a name perhaps derived from the Temple priest during Solomon's time, Zadok, for 10 points what was this aristocratic, priestly clan of Jerusalem, the rivals of the Pharisees?

The decision in this case led to the abandonment of the so-called "Memoirs" test. Hudnut in 1985. Its third prong was narrowed by the holding in Jenkins v. Georgia that the movie Carnal Knowledge could not be found patently offensive solely by the view of community standards regarding pornography. What was this 1973 case, the other two prongs of which stated that for a work to be obscene it had to be patently offensive and lack serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value?

This political organization elected Charles E. Dudley to fill the senate seat vacated by the organization's best-known figure when he took a governorship in 1829. This document clarified the handling of disputes over frankalmoign by mandating jury determination of cases brought before the Assize of Ultram. Another provision moved the adjudication of advowsons from ecclesiastical to secular courts. Restricting the travel out of the country by bishops without the monarch's permission, its promulgator argued for this document's necessity by citing the laity's outrage at the behavior of "criminous clerks." Eight years after the signing of this document, its promulgator was confirmed as Lord of Ireland after humbling himself before Pope Alexander III for his role in the slaying of this document's most vocal opponent. The repudiation of his initial support for what 1164 set of laws enacted by Henry II led directly to the eventual assassination of Thomas a Becket?

Though their sovereignty was established at the Treaty of Berlin, a paramilitary organization of these people sought to reclaim lands taken during the 1908 Annexation Crisis, known as Narodna Odbrana. In an attempt to forestall this event, Andrew Peters appointed a Citizen's Committee chaired by the local reformer, James Storrow, to review the central dispute; however the hard line of Edwin Upton Curtis resulted in the prosecution of 19 individuals, 8 of whom who were indefinitely suspended from work. This event prompted then Governor Calvin Coolidge to tersely conclude, "There is no right to strike against the public safety, anywhere, anytime," name this labor strike beginning on September 9th 1919 set in Massachusetts.

In order to make his increasingly onerous tribute payments, this figure invaded Arussi; additionally, he had to approach the receiver of that tribute face down with a rock on his neck during the "Submission to Yohannes." His wife collaborated in choosing the site of the capital founded by this ruler and Taytu Betul provided its name meaning, "new flower." As a result of his most significant military victory, the Treaty of Wuchale was abrogated, which had previously established his country as a protectorate of a colonial power. Defeating Oreste Baratieri, name this Negus of Shewa who led his country into independence after his victory at Adowa an Emperor of Ethiopia.

Forces could not stop Gellius Egnatius from advancing northward into Etruria during this series of conflicts, and indecisive results by L. Flamma at Volturnus allowed an important coalition to form. During one engagement in this series of conflicts, Gaius Pontius sent ten men dressed as shepherds to feed misinformation to the opposing side that Apulia was under siege, leading T. Veturius' and S. Postumius' forces to be caught in a narrow pass and forced to surrender. Relations prior to the first of this set of conflicts between the eponymous groups began to deteriorate when Christopher Newport attempted to find new trading partners. One engagement which triggered these conflicts involved the ransacking of the burial platforms of the wyroances in a raid led by John Martin. The first of these wars began when George Percy was sent to attack the Pasapahgegh capital. The arrival of the distressed "Third Supply" and the murder of John Ratliffe were the pretexts for the first of these conflicts and the storming and subsequent exile to Tangier Island of Chief Opechancanough's men by William Berkeley ended the second. The victor here benefitted from the loser's dismissal of Greek mercenaries prior to this battle, as the loser had returned home from the winter after a previous inconclusive engagement at Pteria. A speech given by Omer Talon presaged the first phase of this event. The agreement to nullify the king's letters of cachet as well as the July and October declarations of parliament ended the first phase in the Peace of Rueil. That first phase began in earnest with the arrest of Pierre Broussel for leading anti-tax legislation, leading to the second Day of the Barricades in Paris. In anticipation of this man's advancement, Col. John Coming Ball dispatched a sentinel, who heard this leader's horses crossing the Willtown Bridge. This leader nevertheless ordered Maj. Hugh Horrey to attack the Tory flank, while this figure headed east of Dollard's Tavern, during the Battle of Mingo Creek. This man's nemesis conducted the Waxhaw Massacre, helped General Cornwalis to victory at Camden, and attempted to set a trap for this leader at Jack's Ferry. After this man's heroics at Parker's Ferry in August, 1781, this figure was appointed brigadier general, and after the war served in the South Carolina senate. The prelude to this battle saw an aiding army make significant progress, outmaneuvering Publius Scipio in Hispania, and arriving in Gaul later that year. Name this 207 BC battle a decisive Roman victory in the Second Punic War, in which Hasdrubal Barca met his inglorious and headless end.

The losing commander at this battle had just taken control of his country after a viceroy who had previously failed to subdue the Kebbi and quell the Katsina revolt. Oscar Kambona was thought to be this man's most likely successor after he calmed an army mutiny that forced this man and his vice-president Rashid Kawawa into hiding. Aymer de Valence served as mediator between this monarch and his powerful usurping cousin. This victor of the Battle of Boroughbridge had that aforementioned cousin executed soon afterward. This man once received twenty-five dollars from an American, "five for bread and twenty for lead," and he suggested Captain Charles Boycott should be "isolated from his kind as if he were a leper." Survivors of this battle are the protagonists of Jean Larteguy's historical novel The Centurions. This man after having the son of Ariston, his co-regent Damartus, overthrown because he had initially frustrated this man's plans to depose the Aeginetans who had submitted to Persia. After bribing the Delphic Oracle to favor with Leotychides, who became king himself in 491 BCE, this man the son of Anaxandrides II, along with his new co-regent successfully arrested and deposed the Aeginetan collaborators. The smashing of stones produced this site's characteristic discoidal knife, which was named by Gordon Childe for the bay on which this site lies, the Skaill Knife. According to several works by Leonard Carlson, this act was detrimental to farming activity among populations not previously accustomed to the activity. Though this act was repealed by the 1934 Wheeler-Howard Act, the 1906 Burke Act increased the number of forced fee patents issued under this act for the homesteads it provided in order to encourage greater acculturation. One convention prior to this election saw the capitulation of New Jersey Governor George Silzer. The latter convention saw both William McAdoo and Al Smith give up, leading to the nomination of Charles Wayland Brian and John Davis after 103 ballots. Name this Frankish dynasty that spawned Clovis and was replaced by the Carolingians.

In late life this man became known as the "Hermit of Turin." He promulgated the April Laws and, after defeats such as one to Alfred I of Windisch-Grats at the Battle of Schwechat, he released a letter calling his successor Artur Gorgey a "Judas." This author of the "Cassandra" letter created a stir with Queen Victoria and Lord Palmerston in England with speeches inspired by his love of Shakespeare. Jealously hated by Bertalan Szemare, he was a minister in Count Batthyani's government, and appealed to Archduke Franz Joseph of Austria before taking over his country in a fit of Magyar nationalism. Name this Hungarian journalist who briefly led his nation during the Revolutions of 1848.

Eloy Burga's return to this nation sparked conflict with the Pizarro-Rubia casta, partially caused by the discontent Antero Aspillaga, who was cast down by the Partido Civil in favor of Guillermo Billinghurst. Billinghurst was in turn overthrown by the coup of Manuel Prado and Oscar Benavides, and major political parties in this nation's history include the AP of Fernando Belaunde Terry and Victor Raul Haya de la Torre's APRA. This nation was home to the La Cantuta Massacre under a leader who also instituted anti-terrorist policies against the followers of a man calling himself President Gonzalo. Name this country, home to the human rights abuses of both the Shining Path and Alberto Fujimori.

A Sumatran inscription mentioning the merchant guild Nanadesa Tisaiyayirattu Ainnutruvar attests to this polity's trade with Srivijaya. Their artistic productions included the frescoes at Brihadisvara Temple, as well as their lost sculptures and the Airavateswarar Temple. Durings its reign, Kamban wrote the Ramavatharam, and this polity was known for its port city Poompuhar, a center of the powerful navy that allowed them to defeat the Pandya. They overthrew the Pallava and saw the coexistence of Shaivism and Vaishnavism under the rulers who conquered the Kalinga and built temples at Thanjavur, namely, Rajendra and his father Rajaraja. Name this Tamil dynasty that united South India.

Prince Sado of this dynasty was executed by being shut in a rice box, and its cloth tax was decreased by the Kyunyok Law. It suffered the Imo mutiny and signed the Treaty of Ganghwa. Revolts towards the end of its rule included Kyong-nae's Rebellion and the Donghak Uprising, but its decline really began with the assassination of Queen Min. The ruling elite during this dynasty were known as the Yangban, and it was founded by Yi Song-gye. It employed the kobukson designed by Admiral Yi Sin-sin to fight off Japanese invasions, also known as turtle ships. King Sejong introduced Hangul in this dynasty. Name this dynasty which succeeded the Koryo, the longest lasting dynasty of Korea.

One period of this polity's history is known as the Prince Regent Years because Prince Luitpold was forced into power by the madness of his nephew Otto. This polity was restored by the Treaty of Baden after Maximilian II Emanuel's decision to join the French at Blenheim led to its elimination in the Treaty of Ilbersheim. In this region, Anton Arco-Valley assassinated Kurt Eisner, who had set up a republic here in 1918. After Charles Theodore allowed Austria to annex much of this state, Frederick the Great of Prussia forced a return to the status quo at the Treaty of Teschen. Its first king named Ludwig had a dalliance with Lola Montez and its second Ludwig built the castle Neuschwanstein and patronized Wagner. Name this German state which hosted the Beer Hall Putsch in its capital Munich.

One incident during this event saw New Yorkers break into stores to steal barrels of grain. That incident was called the "Flour Riot." Poor farm conditions in Britain led up to this event, which included a 75 percent drop in the price of cotton. It was instigated by an act issued by Levi Woodbury in an attempt to slow inflation and land speculation by requiring the purchase of land in gold or silver. The granting of surplus government funds to pet banks may have contributed to this event along with that act, the Specie Circular. Name this financial crisis that occurred during the presidency of Martin van Buren.

Despite being hit by fifteen separate shells during this battle, the ship Warspite managed to survive it. Hipper and Beatty fought each other at the "Run to the South" phase of this battle, during which the V4 and the Black Prince sank. Those commanders had learned from their earlier battle at Dogger Bank during the previous year. Reinhard Scheer managed to escape at Horn's Reef during this battle, a tactical failure for Admiral John Jellicoe. Despite destroying 115,000 tons of the British fleet, the German goal of assuming control of the North Sea failed. Identify this largest naval battle of the First World War.

One institution blamed for this event was successfully defended in court by the firm of Knox and Reed. Elias Unger, the president of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, tried unsuccessfully to prevent it. Further adding to the chaos was a fire that began at the Stone Bridge. The first major relief effort for Clara Barton's Red Cross, this event was determined to be an "act of God," although many blamed Henry Clay Frick and Andrew Carnegie's resort club for lowering the South Fork Dam. Name this 1889 disaster which killed over 2,000 people and saw torrents of water wipe out a Pennsylvania city.

This nation contains a former residence of the Radzivil Family called Mir Castle, and this nation was the home to the Bielski Brothers. This nation's south contains marshes created by the Pripet River and is the source of the Neman River. This nation contains the Bug River and a fortress on that river was the site of the signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Containing the city of Mahilyow on the Dneiper River and receiving heavy fallout from the Chernobyl disaster, this nation has been led since 1994 by Alexander Lukashenko. Name this former Soviet Republic north of Ukraine sometimes referred to as "White Russia" which has its capital at Minsk.
